Powder
pou´der
n., v. (dust, to grind fine; rendering Hebrew abaq and daq)
From Latin pulvis, dust. To reduce a thing to powder is to make it irrecoverable — the shape cannot be reassembled.

Biblical Definition

Powder is matter ground to dust. Moses treats the golden calf with deliberate thoroughness: he “burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Exo 32:20). Josiah does the same to the idols of Judah (2Ki 23:6). Christ applies the image to Himself as the stone: “on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder” (Mat 21:44), and the Song asks who comes out of the wilderness “perfumed… with all powders of the merchant” (Son 3:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines powder as any dry substance composed of minute particles; and as a verb, to reduce to fine particles, to pulverize, to comminute.

expand to see more

POWDER, n. Any dry substance composed of minute particles, as dust, flour, or the like.

POWDER, v.t. To reduce to fine particles; to comminute; to pulverize; to triturate.

2. To sprinkle with powder.

Key Scripture

Exo 32:20 — "And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it."

2Ki 23:6 — "And he brought out the grove from the house of the LORD, without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped it small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people."

Mat 21:44 — "And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder."

Son 3:6 — "Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?"

Modern Corruption

Idols today are managed, moderated, or renamed; Moses ground his to powder and made the people drink it, on the principle that a repented sin should be made unrecoverable.

expand to see more

Exodus 32:20 is a study in thoroughness. Moses did not confiscate the calf, or store it, or melt it back into usable gold. He burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on the water, and made the people drink the water — so that the idol passed through them and out, and no fragment remained that could be reassembled or quietly retained. Repentance that leaves the material intact is negotiation.

Matthew 21:44 turns the image toward the person of Christ, and the sentence has two halves that cover everyone: whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken; but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder. There is a breaking that a man chooses by falling on the stone in repentance, and a grinding that falls on him. Nobody in the sentence remains unbroken; the only question is which encounter he has.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abaq (H80), fine dust; daq (H1854), to crush small; Greek likmao (G3039), to winnow or grind to powder.

expand to see more

Hebrew daq (H1854) — to crush, beat small; Exodus 32:20, 2 Kings 23:6, ground it to powder.

Hebrew abaq (H80) — fine dust, powder; Song of Solomon 3:6, powders of the merchant.

Greek likmao (G3039) — to grind to powder, scatter as chaff; Matthew 21:44, Luke 20:18.

Usage

"“Ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water” — an idol made unrecoverable."

"“On whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder” — the stone nobody escapes."

"“All powders of the merchant” — the same word for costly fragrance."
